newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Pope urges Czech leaders to heed suffering.
newsitem.headline: Pope urges Czech leaders to heed suffering.

text.p: Pope John Paul called on Saturday for a revival of religion in the Czech Republic and urged the nation's leaders to be sensitive to suffering in society.

The 76-year-old Pontiff, who earlier said mass before a crowd of 50,000 in the town of Hradec Kralove, held private talks with Czech President Vaclav Havel before addressing a meeting of the sick and members of religious communities.

"I would like to address a pressing appeal to the nation's leaders to be constantly sensitive to the situations of suffering present in today's society," the Pope, on his third visit to the Czech Republic, told the meeting.
Civil authorities "should promote effective and constant solidarity within society," he said.
The Czech Republic has one of the highest standards of living in the former East bloc but the Pope said on Friday it faced "a growing crisis of values".
Earlier, Havel and his wife, Dagmar, whom he married in February, greeted the Pontiff at Prague Castle, handing him a lily before their talks.
Havel, a former dissident playwright seen by many as the nation's leading moral authority, has frequently called for spiritual renewal in a highly secular society.

In Hradevc Karlove, some 100 km (60 miles) east of Prague, the Pope told a crowd of mainly young people that four decades of communist persecution had left the faithful feeling like the early Christians.
"The church needs you," he told the crowd in a sermon as they braved drizzle to see him in a square framed by baroque buildings and the town's Cathedral of the Holy Spirit.
A sea of yellow and white Vatican flags went up as he was driven through the square in a bullet-proof "Popemobile".
"After 40 years of attempts to silence her, she (the church) is experiencing here among you a wonderful revival, even in the midst of many difficulties," he said.
"You are living in a situation that, under certain aspects, is like the situation of the first Christians," he said, adding that young people had to begin spreading the faith anew.

Relations between the Catholic Church and the state in the former Czechoslovakia, which split peacefully in 1993 into the Czech and Slovak republics, were among the worst in the former East bloc. Many of its leaders were harshly persecuted, its churches closed and priests arrested.
The crowd interrupted his sermon repeatedly with chants of "We love you," bringing smiles to his face. He joked several times with the young people.
The Pontiff, who has suffered a series of health problems in recent years, appeared in relatively good form, reading his sermon in Czech in a strong voice as the rain fell.
However, his left hand shook in what is widely believed to be a sign he is suffering from Parkinson's disease.
The main purpose of the trip is to mark the 1,000th anniversary of the death of St Adalbert, who brought Christianity to Bohemia, now part of the Czech Republic, and to the Pope's native Poland.

St Adalbert is seen by the church as "an apostle of Europe" and the Pope is expected to use a mass on Sunday in Prague to evoke the saint in a call for the continent to seek unity based on its common Christian roots.
